Sultan Ahmed with Malik Syed Ahmed, Advocates — for the Petitioner 
Syed Motiul Islam, Assistant Attorney-General —For the State
parties:
Nuruddin Ahmed Sajal ----- Petitioner
VS.
State  ----- opposite Party
full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam J : This Rule arises out of an application filed by the petitioner under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure for quashing the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 2.4.1994 passed by the Judge, Anti-Terrorism Additional Tribunal No. 3, Dhaka in Anti-Terrorism Case No. 314 of 1993 arising out of Dhanmondi Police Case Case No. 3(a)/93 GR Case No. 4136 of 1993. 

 2. The prosecution case, in short, is that informant PW 1 Saker Ansari, Manager Seven-Eleven and Saiham Sweets, Shop No. 2, Road No. 12, Mirpur Road, Dhanmondi, Dhaka on 1.9.93 at 16.15 hours lodged an First Information Report in Dhanmondi Police Station alleging that the students of Sukrabad New Model Degree College, Nuruddin Ahmed Sajal, Farid Ahmed Majumder Pintu, Mahbubur Rahman Kiron. Milton, Titus, Sujan and some students of Dhaka Dental College Hospital numbering about 15/20, who will be recognized if seen again, suddenly entered 'Seven-Eleven' and Pintu, Sajal and Kiron asked him to come out from cash (counter). He came out in good faith and immediately thereafter accused Pintu, Sajal and Kiron along with two others suddenly pulled out arms and by a show of terroristic attitude terrorized him, employees of his shop, wayfarers and forcibly got him on a rickshaw and took him to Dental College Hospital. There the accused persons searched his body, snatched Taka 1200.00 (twelve hundred) from his pocket. They on point of arms such as cut rifle, Kax Knife, etc, took LTI and signatures in two white papers and also took photo giving the said cut-rifle and knife in his hand. They also gave threat to the informant that if he lodges First Information Report in the Thana, then, they will finish him in life. They perpetrated for about 30 minutes inhuman torture on him putting him in fear of death. Thereafter they let him off. He came to his shop and found the door, show case, chair, table everything in bro ken condition. The accused Sajal, Kiron and their associates at many a times ate without paying bills and when the money was demanded they threatened him. 

 The accused petitioner Nuruddin Ahmed Sajal was tried in absentia along with four others of whom Mahbubur Rahman alias Kiron was also tried in absentia. The defence case as it appears from the trend of cross examination is that there was mismanagement of cash money over which an unpleasant incident took place between the owner and employees of the shop. That the accused persons have been falsely implicated in this case and they have not done anything of this nature. They pleaded not guilty of the charge and claimed to be tried. 

 Of the 12 PWs informant PW 1 is the Manager and relation (Bhatija) of PW 8 (uncle of PW 1) owner of the shop Seven Eleven PW 2, 3 (Assistant Manager), 4 (Cashier), 5, 6, 7 are the employees of the shop. PW 9 was tendered but not cross examined by the defence, PW 10 AK Nazmul, Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka recorded on the direction of CMM statements of PW 1(Exhibit-2) PW 2 (Exhibit-4) PW 3 (Exhibit-5) PW 4 (Exhibit-6) PW 5(Exhibit-7) PW 6 (Exhibit-8) PW 7 (Exhibit-9) PW 8 (Exhibit-10). PW 11 OC Dhanmondi PS investigated the case in part and PW 12 Inspector of Police after investigation submitted charge sheet on 14.10.1993. 

 4. The case was thereafter sent to Anti-Terrorism Tribunal No.3 Dhaka for trial. Since the petitioner was absconding all through the trial was held in absentia after complying with the necessary legal formalities. The learned Judge of the Anti-Terrorism Tribunal at the conclusion of the trial found this accused petitioner guilty of the charge and convicted and sentenced him thereunder to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six years and to pay a fine of Taka 500.00 in default to suffer RI for 15 days more by the judgment and order dated 2.4.1994. 

 5. The accused petitioner submits that he was quite in darkness about the case, his trial in absentia and conviction and sentence until his arrest by the police on 6.8.1994 and he was not absconding. Had he been in the know of the case against him he as a law abiding citizen would have appeared before the tribunal to give his defence. Thus being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and conviction and sentence the petitioner has preferred this application under section 561A of the CrPC. 

 7. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, first of all has taken us through the First Information Report, the deposition of the witnesses and other materials on record including the impugned judgment. Thereafter he assails the conviction and sentence of the petitioner on various grounds. He firstly, contends that the ingredients of the alleged charge as against the petitioner have not been satisfactorily proved by the prosecution beyond all reasonable doubt by sufficient and reliable evidence. It is submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that in this case in fact, PWs. 1-3 are the only material witnesses who are said to have proved the allegations against the accused petitioner and PW 1 is the only material witness to prove the extraction of alleged donation from him by the accused persons but these three witnesses, according to Mr. Ahmed, are highly interested and partisan, and there are material contradictions in their evidences, as such their evidences ought not to have been relied on. He further submits that the learned Anti-Terrorism Tribunal without properly appreciating and duly scanning the evidence on record in its true perspective and without proper application of the judicial mind to the materials on record has wrongly found the PWs. as trustworthy and most illegally convicted and sentenced the accused petitioner and, as such, the conviction and sentence of the petitioner is an abuse of the process of Court which for the ends of justice should be quashed. It is further submitted by Mr. Ahmed that all the prosecution witnesses are highly interested and partisan witnesses. To secure the conviction of the petitioner not a single independent, disinterested and trustworthy witness even of the locality has been examined. He, therefore, contends that the prosecution has not been able to prove the case against the petitioner by reliable and sufficient evidence vis-a-vis the place, time and manner of occurrence. Further contention of the learned lawyer of the petitioner is, that the finding of the learned Tribunal that at the leadership of the petitioner and another absconding accused Kiron the incident took place is absolutely beyond the evidence on record. The final submission of Mr. Ahmed is that an attempt to realise money in the form of donation or otherwise is not a punishable offence under the Anti-Terrorism Act. 

 9. Let us now consider the respective submissions of the learned Advocates of both the parties in the light of the evidence and materials on record. It is one of the submissions of Mr. Ahmed that there is departure from the First Information Report story and there is embellishment of prosecution story. It is true that First Information Report being the earliest record of the case it has got much importance. It enables the court to see what the prosecution case was when it was started and to check up any subsequent embellishment or any departure therefrom as the case proceeds through different stages. In fact prosecution story hibernates in the First Information Report in incubation and the same may be unfolded at the subsequent time during the trial through the process of evidence. Although First Information Report cannot be used as substantive evidence, the same may be taken resort to only for the purpose of comparison with the story subsequently developed during trial in order to bring out the conflict between the prosecution versions. Any departure or deviation from the main story disclosed at the earliest recorded version may be looked upon with great suspicion. 

 10. In the present case, it is to be noticed that the prosecution has recorded its version in the First Information Report giving out the story that the accused persons suddenly entered into the shop "Seven-Eleven" and the petitioner and two others asked the informant to come out from cash counter, he came out in good faith and immediately thereafter the accused Pintu, Kiron and the petitioner along with two others suddenly pulled out arms and by a show of terroristic attitude terrorized him employees of his shop, wayfaers and forcibly got him on a rickshaw and took him to Dental College Hospital. There the accused persons searched his body, snatched Taka 1200,00.(twelve hundred) from his pocket. They on point of arms such as cut-rifle, knife, etc. took LTI and signature in two white papers and also took photograph giving the said cut-rifle and knife in his hand. They also gave threat to the informant that if he lodges a First Information Report in the Thana, then they will finish him in life. They perpetrated for about 30 minutes inhuman torture on him putting him in fear of life. Thereafter let him off. He came back to his shop and found the door, showcase, chair, table everything in broken condition. 

 "But during the trial the prosecution has made out a different case ১.৯.৯৩ ইং তারিখ বেলা ১১.০০ টা সময় সজল, কিরন, পিন্টু, মিল্টন, তিতাস ও অন্যান্যরা ২০/২৫ জন আমার সেভেন ইলেভেন পেষ্ট্রা সপে ঢোকে । সজল আমাকে ডাকে এবং বাহিরে আসেন কথা আছে। আমি বাহির হইলে তখন সজল, কিরন ও ২/৩ জন রিক্সায় উঠায় এবং ডেন্টাল কলেজ হোষ্টেলে লইয়া যায়। সেখানে আমার নিকট হইতে ৫০,০০০ টাকা চাঁদা দাবী করে। আমি অস্বীকৃতি জানাইলে তারা কাটা রাইফেল ধরিয়া সাদা কাগজে টিপ ও স্বাক্ষর লয়। আমার হাতে অস্ত্র দিয়া ছবি ও তাহারা তোলে। কতক্ষন বসাইয়া রাখিয়া ছাড়িয়া দেয়। দোকানে আসিয়া দেখি যে, দরজার গ্লাস, টেবিল, প্লেট, জগ, আসবাবপত্র ভাংগিয়া চুরমার করিয়াছে।” 

 11. Thus we find that during the trial the prosecution has made a departure from the mainstream of the prosecution story as stated in the First Information Report and introduced an altogether new story of demanding chanda of Taka 50,000 First Information Report is the foundation of the prosecution case and if the foundation is removed, the whole prosecution case shall fall. The witnesses for the prosecution are to support the prosecution case appearing in the First Information Report. If being motivated or for some other reasons, the witnesses shrink from the mainstream of the prosecution story and deposed differently on essential particulars, the witnesses are liable to be disbelieved. 

 12. In the present case we find that there is a substantial departure of the prosecution case from the first recorded version which creates doubt. Partial departure from the First Information Report makes the prosecution case shaky and the same may be looked upon with great suspicion. It will not be safe to rely on the evidence of witnesses who are found to be unworthy of credence relating to one part of the prosecution story in material particulars. It is elementary that where the prosecution has a definite or positive case, it must prove the whole of it. Therefore, partial departure affects the credibility of the witnesses very much. This aspect of the case has been completely ignored by the learned Tribunal 

 13. In this case the prosecution has examined 12 witnesses out of which PW 9 was tendered. PWs 1-7 are alleged to be eye witnesses of the occurrence. PW 8 is the owner of the shop and he did not see the occurrence. PW 10 is the Magistrate who recorded the 164 statements of the PWs. 11 and 12 are the investigating officers of these witnesses. The evidence of PWs.1-3 are relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule in as much as the other eye-witness did not say anything in their evidence about the occurrence. According PW 1, Kiron, the petitioner and 2/3 other persons got him on a rickshaw and took him to Dental College Hospital and there they demanded Chanda (donation) of Taka 50,000.00 from him. PW 2 stated in his evidence that 2/3 persons brought PW 1 out of the ship and took him away by a rickshaw. The rest had broken the furniture’s. Sajal (the petitioner before us) Kiron, Milton, Titas, Pintu and others did this. But this witness in his cross categorically stated that the accuseds present in the dock were not the persons who had broken the furniture’s. On the other hand, PW 3 stated that Milton, Kiron and Sajal (the petitioner) forcibly took PW 1 to Dental College Hostel, Pintu, Titas, Sujan and others broke the furniture’s. These are all the evidence against the petitioner. On an analysis of the evidence we find that PW 1 is contradicted by PW 2 in that PW 1 stated that amongst others the petitioner was also there who took him forcibly away from the shop whereas PW 2 stated that the petitioner was amongst them who broke the furniture’s in the shop. This material contradiction has been lost sight of by the learned Tribunal. The evidence of PW 3 does not disclose any offence under section 4 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. It thus appears that there is absolutely no evidence involving the petitioner within the alleged offence charged but the learned Tribunal on a misreading of the evidence wrongly found the accused petitioner guilty of the charge which is not tenable in law. We find that it is a case of no evidence at all. It also appears that PW 1 did not state in the First Information Report that he reported to PW 8 that Pintu, Mintu, Sajal and others took him away from the shop nor he made any such statements in his deposition before the Tribunal whereas PW 8 stated in his examination-in-chief that PW 1 stated that Pintu, Mintu, Sajal and others took him away from the shop. This piece of evidence is per-se inadmissible in as much as PW 1 did not assert in his deposition that he told so to PW 8 nor the same fact is mentioned in the First Information Report. PW 8 in his cross examination stated that the did not mention the name of any accused including the name of the petitioner before the Magistrate in his 164 statement. Moreover the deposition of PW 8 is contradictory to the deposition of PW. 1 in-as-much as PW 1 stated that the accused persons demanded chanda of Taka 50,000.00 (donation) from him whereas PW 8 stated that the accused persons forcibly took PW 1 to the Dental College hostel and snatched money from him, tortured him, took his photograph and also obtained signature in blank paper. So, the evidence of PW 1 and PW 8 are contradictory to each other and highly incongruous. The learned Judge of the Tribunal failed to appreciate this aspect of the case and wrongly relied on the evidence of this PW. in arriving at a finding of guilt of the petitioner. 

 14. There is another aspect of the case, To bring the petitioner within the mischief of section 2 (2)(ক) of the Anti-Terrorism Act, there must be snatching away of something namely, money, ornaments valuables or  of any vehicle or material by force by the petitioner and also to bring him under an offence under section 2(2)(ক) of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1992, there must be creation of terror, disorder, lawlessness by individually or collectively showing or exhibiting force in any place, house, shop hat-bazar, roads, vehicles or institutions in a planned way or suddenly. We have already discussed the material evidence and also quoted the relevant evidence given by PW 1 before the Tribunal. If we carefully examine the facts and circumstances of the instant case and the evidence on record, it is difficult for us to hold that the petitioner created any such disorder or lawlessness or any terror in the alleged shop by showing, using or exhibiting any force suddenly or in a planned way individually or collectively or that he snatched any money from the person of the PW 1 at the Dental College Hostel. There is no evidence at all to that effect in this case. Thus considering the entire evidence on record, we are of the view that the prosecution has not been able to bring home the charge against the accused petitioner by cogent and reliable evidence beyond all reasonable doubt. 

 15. There is another interesting point of law in the instant case. In the previous paragraphs we have extensibly quoted the First Information Report case as well as the case made out at the trial. It is no doubt that the story as narrated in the First Information Report does constitute offence under the Anti-Terrorism Act 1992. But the case as is made out in the evidence does not come within the ambit of the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1992. We have already quoted the evidence of PW 1 as given before the learned Tribunal. The evidence of PW 1 read with the evidence of other witnesses does not show that the petitioner along with others forcibly realised chanda (donation) from the informant PW 1. There was, according to PW 1, merely an attempt to realise chanda from him. The moot question, therefore, in this case is whether a mere demand for donation is an offence as defined in the Anti-Terrorism Act, 1992, for an attempt has not been made an offence under the said Act which is a special law. Section 2(2)(315) of the said Act defines the offence in the following terms: 

 16. Under section 5 of the Act abetment has been made an offence but attempt to realise any money in the form of chanda (donation) or otherwise has not been included within the definition of the offence. It is now well settled that in a special law an offence must be specifically provided. It has been decided in the case of Md. Akram and another vs. State, reported in AIR 1951 (Assam) 17 that "Unless an attempt to commit an offence under a special or local law has been expressly made punishable it cannot be punished under the Penal Code as section 511 of the Penal Code is omitted from section 40 thereof". Similarly in 33 DLR 379 in the case of Abdul Halim Pattader and others vs. M. Rahmat Ali & others this Division has held that " Abetment is an offence by itself and unless it is specifically made punishable in a special Act a person cannot be called upon to answer a charge of abetment in the absence of any special provision in the special Act merely by the reference of the Penal Code. In the instant case admittedly mere demand for chanda (donation) was made but it was not realised. In these circumstances the simple question is whether the charge as framed under section 4 of the Anti-Terrorism Act can be at all levelled against the accused petitioners as the offence was not complete. We have carefully examined the relevant provision of the Act and we find that an attempt to realise chanda (donation) from a person is not made an offence within the meaning of "Anti-terrorism Act" and as such the charge levelled against the accused petitioner is quashed. 

 17. On a perusal of the impugned judgment it appears that the learned Tribunal did not apply its judicial mind to the facts and circumstances of the case. It appears that the learned Tribunal found that at the leadership of the petitioner and another absconding accused Kiron the incident took place. We find that this finding of the learned Tribunal is perverse and it is based on mere surmise and conjecture only and not borne out by the materials and evidence on record. 

 18. It also appears that the learned Tribunal failed to appreciate the fact that all the prosecution witnesses are highly interested and partisan and to secure the conviction of the petitioner not a single independent, disinterested and trustworthy witness even of the locality has been examined in this case. 

 19. After considering all the aspects of the case we are of opinion that if the conviction is maintained in the instant case that would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court and for the ends of justice the same should be quashed. 

 20. In the result the Rule is made absolute and the judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 2.4.1994 passed by the Judge, Anti-Terrorism Additional Tribunal No. 3, Dhaka in Anti-Terrorism Case No. 314 of 1993 arising out of Dhanmondi PS Case No. 3(9)/93, GR Case No. 4186 of 1993 convicting and sentencing the accused petitioner is quashed so far it relates to the petitioner and the petitioner Nuruddin Ahmed Sajal, son of late M A Mollick is acquitted and he be set at liberty at once if not wanted in connection with any other case.
